https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgjq.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, The fire appears to have been put out but smouldering ruins remain By Emery Makumeno ,Â BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Kinshasa Â and Â Robert Greenall Published 10 September 2026 At least 24 schoolchildren have died in a stampede as they tried to flee a fire that engulfed two schools in rebel-held Bukavu in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, officials there have said. Adults are also reported to have died in the fire and there are fears that the death toll could rise further in the densely populated Kadutu commune. Survivors have been taken to nearby hospitals, and footage of the scene shows children lying on hospital floors in pain. Some 300 houses have also been destroyed in the fire, the cause of which is unknown. Rebelâappointed authorities released a provisional death toll of 24 on Thursday evening, confirming previous reports, but there are fears that more people may have died. Pictures circulating on social media show young children lying motionless on the ground. A witness quoted by Reuters news agency said the fire had been put out by afternoon but smoke was still rising from rubble and corrugated metal. Bukavu, the capital of South Kivu province and one of DR Congo's most crowded hillside cities, was captured by M23 rebels in February last year. Meanwhile the government in Kinshasa released a statement on X, without specifying numbers of casualties. "The Ministry of National Education and New Citizenship expressed deep sorrow over the deadly fire," it said. "With several lives lost and many injured, the toll remains provisional. The minister offered condolences, affirmed solidarity with families, and ordered assessments of affected schools to ensure learning continuity." The tragedy follows a similar fire in Kinshasa last weekend, where residents died in a stampede at a wedding banquet hall. In response, the government has ordered strict safety measures and deployed teams nationwide to enforce standards at public gathering places. https://www.politico.eu/article/andy-bur.text: LONDON — Andy Burnham has his work cut out to convince voters the U.K. should change the way it elects MPs, according to a new POLITICO Poll. This week the prime minister vowed to come up with proposals to ditch the first-past-the-post voting system, which has been used in British general elections since 1884, to provide more political stability and a system that is fairer to all voters. But a survey by pollsters Public First, conducted before Burnham’s announcement, found that 57% of respondents regard first-past-the-post as a “mostly” or “completely” fair way to decide elections. (A majority of voters across parties feel this way.) Advertisement Advertisement At the same time, the survey revealed potential openness to a system of proportional representation, in which the number of parliamentary seats each party wins is more closely linked to the total number of votes it receives across the country. “Most people don’t spend much time thinking about how we elect MPs and, broadly, people think the current system is fair,” said Seb Wride, head of polling at Public First. “Burnham will need to make a convincing case to voters about why changing the electoral system is necessary, if he is to gain support for his plans.” Under first-past-the-post, whichever candidate wins the most votes in their constituency is elected to represent that seat, even if they fall far short of a majority of local voters. Nationally, that can result in a party taking power with relatively low popular support. Labour won the last election in 2024 by a landslide, taking 63% of seats in Parliament with just 34% of the vote — the most disproportionate result in British history. Since then, some polling projections have suggested Nigel Farage’s populist-right Reform UK party was on track to win a majority with around 30% of votes under the first-past-the-post system. In a speech to Labour members in Liverpool, Burnham said recent turbulence in British politics — he’s the country’s seventh prime minister in 10 years — meant a new system was needed. “We will all have failed in our public duties if we carry on as we are and open the door of No. 10 to a divisive government on less than 30% of the vote,” he said. Advertisement Advertisement How to choose Many voting systems could replace first-past-the-post, some based on a form of proportional representation (PR). Public First’s analysis found that support for moving to PR varied depending on which party was proposing it. When Labour voters were shown a Labour proposal to move to PR, 54% supported the idea, whereas when they were shown an identical proposal branded as coming from Reform UK, only 36% supported it. The same broad pattern was true of Reform voters. A man walks past a fallen placard as he exits a polling station after casting his vote in the local elections on May 7, 2026 in Surbiton, England. | Carl Court/Getty Images Overall, 41% of U.K. adults responding to the poll said they would “somewhat” support or “strongly support” a Labour proposal to move toward PR. Another 26% would neither support nor oppose it, and 22% somewhat opposed or strongly opposed the idea. “While they lean toward supporting reform, many voters judge it by who is proposing it,” said Wride. “With trust in politicians so low, if electoral reform looks like just one party’s project, it risks being seen as political game-playing.” Burnham’s pledge on electoral reform could boost his chances of staying in power, but much could change ahead of the next election, which could take place as late as 2029. Polls currently predict a hung parliament with Labour falling short of a majority, but the Liberal Democrats have long campaigned for electoral reform and would be Labour’s most likely coalition partners. Farage has also spoken in favor of replacing first-past-the-post with an alternative voting system, but has recently said less on the topic. This week, the party’s deputy leader Richard Tice said it was “no time” to be discussing electoral reform. Advertisement Advertisement One person familiar with the thinking in Burnham’s team said they expected the government preference would be for the same “ supplementary vote ” system used in Greater Manchester mayoral elections. It allows voters to pick a second preference — with those votes being counted if the lead candidate doesn’t win at least 50% of first preference votes. Separately, a government official said a “constituency link” in any new voting system would be “critical” for Burnham. “I found it better being elected under a different system as mayor of Greater Manchester where people had one or two — they could put that on the ballot paper,” Burnham told the BBC this week. “Because you had a reason to stop on every doorstep and chat to people who might not always support your party and try and get their second preference. It just led to a better politics.” Sam Blewett and Emilio Casalicchio contributed reporting. Public First surveyed 2,028 U.K. adults online Sept. 13-15, 2026.

https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/10/23/okto.text: Menü Kereső Ránk számíthattok! 3000 új támogatót keresünk Csatlakozom Betyárok, agresszorok, Gripenek és Párizs – mindenki máshogyan értette 1956-ot Belföld Fotó Németh Sz. Péter Zagyi Tibor Bakró-Nagy Ferenc Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom „Hosszú éveken át azt hazudták nekünk, hogy a nemzeti ünnep csak egy politikai oldalnak jár, de ennek vége” – mondta október 23-i ünnepi beszédében Magyar Péter az „immár tényleg független Magyarországot” köszöntve. Orbán Viktort Párizsban fotózták le, így a Fidesz nélküle ünnepelt. A párt szerint egy szabad országban a hatalom nem fenyeget senkit letartóztatással, és nincsenek politikai foglyok sem, így küzdelmes, kutyanehéz évek állnak előttünk. Az '56-os forradalom 70. évfordulója képekben. Szokás szerint a Parlament épülete előtti ünnepélyes zászlófelvonással kezdődtek meg az október 23-i programok, a zászlófelvonást díszmenet követte. António Costa, az Európai Tanács elnöke, Ursula von der Leyen , az Európai Bizottság elnöke, valamint Jens Stoltenberg, Norvégia pénzügyminisztere, a NATO volt főtitkára is hivatalos volt a Parlament díszülésére, ahol Forsthoffer Ágnes tartott megemlékezést. „Ma Budapesten dobog a világ szíve” – mondta a házelnök. Baka András államfő szerint a megemlékezésnek külön jelentőséget ad a megjelent külföldi vendégek jelenléte, a magyar forradalomnak 70 éve egyetemes jelentősége van, és az európai egység megteremtésére is hatott. A Kossuth téren, az 1956-os állami ünnepségen 56 harangszóval emlékeztek meg a 70 éve kitört forradalomról, Magyar Péter beszéde előtt Gripenek repültek át a tér felett. „Aki egy agresszort menteget, vagy idegen birodalmaknak rendelné alá a nemzetet, az semmit sem ért 1956 üzenetéből” – mondta Magyar Péter miniszterelnök közel egyórás beszédében . Azt mondta, volt tizenhárom dicsőséges nap, amikor a magyarok egységesen kiáltották, hogy ruszkik, haza! Arról is beszélt, hogy „hosszú éveken át azt hazudták nekünk, hogy a nemzeti ünnep csak egy politikai oldalnak jár, de ennek vége”. Szerinte jó lenne olyan országot hagyni a gyerekeinkre, amire büszkék lehetünk. „Ez itt a mi hazánk, és mi bármire képesek vagyunk érte” – mondta. A Fidesz szimpatizánsai Békemenet helyett Zászlómenetet tartottak, a menet betyárok ostorcsapásaira indult meg dél körül a Műegyetem elől. Egy huszár vezette őket, mögötte a betyárok következtek, majd sorban a felvonulók, akik két oldalról fogták az 1848 méteres zászlót. Egy ideig teljes csendben vonultak a budai alsó rakparton, később énekelni kezdtek, főleg a Nélküledet, de a Gábor Áron rézagyúja is felcsendült. A Bem térre érve már többen gyűltek össze, mint a Fidesz megmozdulásain az elmúlt hónapokban. A korábbi évekkel ellentétben Orbán Viktor idén nem mondott ünnepi beszédet, ehelyett Párizsban üldögélt egy hotel teraszán , miközben a Facebook-oldala élőben adta a Bem téri eseményt. Beszédet mondott Bóka János, a Fidesz frakcióvezetője, Áder János volt köztársasági elnök, és Schmidt Mária történész is. Áder szerint ha egy szóval kéne összefoglalnia, hogy miből lett elegük az embereknek ’56-ban, akkor a hazugságot mondaná. Demokrácia helyett diktatúra, szabadság helyett szolgaság, gyarapodás helyett szegénység, egyenlőség helyett új nomenklatúra. Bóka János arról beszélt, hogy egy szabad országban nem állítanak fel politikai rendőrséget, a hatalom nem fenyeget senkit letartóztatással, nem mutogatnak senkit bilincsben a hatalom utasítására, és nincsenek politikai foglyok sem, szabad országban nem akarják felszámolni az ellenzéket. Beszéde közben a fideszes résztvevők ellentüntetőkkel feszültek össze , akiket a rendőrségnek kellett megvédenie. A Telex stábját is megtámadták . Baka András, Magyar Péter és Forsthoffer Ágnes a nemzeti lobogó ünnepélyes felvonásán az 1956-os forradalom és szabadságharc 70. évfordulóján az Országház előtti Kossuth Lajos téren 2026. október 23-án – Fotó: Máthé Zoltán / MTI A Mi Hazánk és csatolt szervezetei a Corvin közben emlékeztek meg, 1956 mellett a 2006-os tévészékházostrom 20. évfordulójáról is. Felszólalt többek között Novák Előd és Toroczkai László is, a beszédekben a háttérhatalomról, a globalistákról, az LMBTQ-lobbiszervezetekről, a választásokba való beavatkozásról volt szó, de rengetegszer elhangzott von der Leyen és Magyar Péter neve is. https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.text: Benjamin Netanyahu first become prime minister 30 years ago and has held the office for more than 19 years. Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images/AFP View image in fullscreen Benjamin Netanyahu first become prime minister 30 years ago and has held the office for more than 19 years. Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images/AFP The Saturday read Israel As a divided Israel prepares to go to the polls, can Netanyahu pull off his greatest political trick yet? The prime minister has defined and dominated his country’s politics for three decades and is putting his rivals on the defensive before Tuesday’s general election Jonathan Freedland in Modi’in Sat 24 Oct 2026 01.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 01.02 EDT Share They chant his name, they cheer and clap – and yet he is not the most dominant person in the room. Looming over the crowd that has gathered to hear Gadi Eisenkot, the former general who is the lead opposition challenger in Tuesday’s Israeli election, is a man who is not there. It is the man Eisenkot seeks to replace as prime minister, the man who first served in that role three decades ago and who has held it, on and off, for 19 of the past 30 years. It is Benjamin Netanyahu . Naturally, the warm-up speakers at this evening rally in the modest city of Modi’in, halfway between Tel Aviv and Jerusalem, stress the virtues of Eisenkot, a son of working-class Moroccan Jews who rose through the ranks to become chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces and entered politics only four years ago. But every sentence might as well end with two words that go unspoken: unlike Bibi . View image in fullscreen Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief of staff and head of the Yashar party, delivers an address on the campaign trail. In an obvious reference to Benjamin Netanyahu, he has called for a ‘country without lies’. Photograph: Ilia Yefimovich/AFP/Getty Images Even the name of Eisenkot’s party, Yashar, meaning straight or direct, carries the implied contrast with Netanyahu, who is regarded by friends and enemies alike as a maestro of the darkest political arts. When Eisenkot calls for “a country without lies”, when he calls for “responsibility and leading by example”, when he suggests US-style term limits for the role of prime minister, “because power corrupts”, everyone knows what – and who – he means. None of this comes with rhetorical fire or theatrical panache. But the lack of charisma serves only to emphasise that Eisenkot is every inch the un-Bibi. “I think that’s an advantage,” Noa Sadeh, 56, told me after Wednesday night’s rally. “I’m fed up with people who know how to talk – like Bibi. We need someone who will do the doing part.” Spotting a journalist with a notebook, David Nadler, 74, a retired colonel who served under Eisenkot, insisted I write down the word “integrity”, meaning “he says something, he means it, he will do it”. Another sentence ending with those silent words: unlike Bibi . View image in fullscreen Eisenkot shakes hands with Netanyahu at a swearing-in ceremony in Jerusalem in 2015 attended by the then defence minister, Moshe Ya’alon. Eisenkot has pledged to wipe out Hamas. Photograph: Menahem Kahana/AFP/Getty Images It’s hard to overstate Netanyahu’s dominance not only over this campaign but over Israeli politics and political culture. The two blocs in this election are not left and right but Bibi and anti-Bibi. The latter camp includes at least two figures – the former PM Naftali Bennett and the Moldova-born Avigdor Lieberman – whose natural home is on the nationalist right and who both once worked closely with Netanyahu, only to fall out with him spectacularly. Almost every political figure is defined, or defines themselves, in relation to Netanyahu. Eisenkot offers himself as the antidote, but listen to the pitch made by the far right and it too is all about the prime minister. Netanyahu is like a shopping trolley, says Yishai Fleisher, of Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) party, to a group of about 30 orthodox voters in a study hall in Bet Shemesh on Thursday evening. “He has a tendency to go left, so you have to pull him to the right.” Fleischer makes the case for yet more Jewish settlements in the West Bank, to say nothing of settling Gaza; for a “ministry of emigration” that will encourage the “voluntary” departure of Palestinians; for the death penalty; for ever harsher treatment of Palestinian prisoners; for putting more guns and more ammunition into the hands of Jewish Israeli civilians – but all in the context of strengthening the resolve of a new Netanyahu-led coalition. On the right, Ben-Gvir is a moon that is rising, but Netanyahu is still the sun. View image in fullscreen Itamar Ben-Gvir, centre, the leader of the Jewish Power party, on the campaign trail in Ramla. The far-right politician is calling for more Jewish settlements in the West Bank and harsh measures against Palestinians. Photograph: Amir Cohen/Reuters Partly, that’s a function of sheer longevity. But it’s also down to Netanyahu’s undimmed ability to set the political agenda. Even in this election, he has demarcated the terrain on which battle is fought. His latest poster campaign offers voters a rhyming choice of Yamin , meaning the right, or Falastin , meaning Palestine. On the right side is, of course, his own face and the Israeli flag; on the other, the leaders of the opposition parties, including Bennett and Lieberman who are adamantly opposed to a Palestinian state, all of them surrounding two heads of parties that represent Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about a fifth of the country’s population. The message is not subtle: vote for me, or you’ll get the Arabs. View image in fullscreen Netanyahu campaign posters are put on display in Jerusalem. The prime minister is pitching the election as a choice between himself and the Arabs. Photograph: Kevin Coombs/Reuters Indeed, the closing weeks of the campaign have centred on the question of whether the anti-Netanyahu bloc of Jewish Israeli parties – currently forecast to do better than the Netanyahu bloc but to fall short of an overall majority in the Knesset – will do some kind of parliamentary deal with the mainly Arab parties, most of which have, historically, both refused to join Israeli governments and not been invited. Backed by that chunk of the media that is loudly and vociferously pro-Netanyahu, most notably the Fox News wannabe Channel 14, Netanyahu has succeeded in putting his opponents on the defensive. A rare exception to that pattern came just this week when a Netanyahu uber-loyalist, Channel 14’s Yinon Magal, characterised Eisenkot as a Moroccan “monkey” . The racial slur was so crude that had it been used by the left to describe a politician of the right, it would have had Netanyahu denouncing Ashkenazi elitism from the rooftops (even though Netanyahu is, of course, a privileged scion of the Ashkenazi elite). Tellingly, while the warm-up speakers in Modi’in mentioned the “monkey” remark, Eisenkot himself did not. To his admirers, that was the mark of a decent man reluctant to follow his opponents into the gutter. To the doubters, it was a sign of a politician still playing by Marquess of Queensbury rules – one who doesn’t quite appreciate what, or rather who, he is up against. For an outside observer, the most puzzling question about this Israeli election is: how is this even close? How can the polls be showing the two blocs, pro- and anti-Netanyahu, neck and neck? Abroad, many will be baffled that Netanyahu can still be in contention given the devastation his government brought down upon Gaza , flattening much of the territory and killing more than 70,000 Palestinians, even if, as Israel says, one-third of them were Hamas combatants. But even inside Israel, where the impact of the war on the people of Gaza is all too rarely discussed, it is no less of a riddle that Netanyahu is a serious candidate in these elections, let alone one who could emerge on top. View image in fullscreen Eisenkot, who entered politics only four years ago, is defining himself as the anti-Netanyahu candidate in Tuesday’s election. Photograph: Jack Guez/AFP/Getty Images To start with the most elemental fact, the biggest disaster in the country’s history happened on his watch. The massacres inflicted on civilian Israel on 7 October 2023, at the Nova music festival and at a string of southern kibbutzim, are still fresh in the memory. Stickers depicting the faces of those killed on that day adorn bus stops and railway platforms from one end of the country to the other. As Oded Levi, who voted for Netanyahu in 2022 but was in the Modi’in crowd for Eisenkot, put it: “Whoever was prime minister [then] is responsible. He has to go. For this reason alone, we need a change.” But it hardly ends there. Netanyahu promised a war that would destroy and eradicate Hamas. That didn’t happen. Instead, Israel destroyed its own international reputation, leaving the country isolated and fast becoming a pariah state. Netanyahu promised to destroy Iran’s nuclear threat and that too didn’t happen. View image in fullscreen Raz Zarfati at a memorial to her sister, Ron, who was killed in the 7 October attacks. Netanyahu has shifted blame for the disaster. Photograph: Ohad Zwigenberg/AP Add to that the “judicial coup” in the months before 7 October, where Netanyahu tried to weaken the restraint on his power represented by the supreme court, thereby splitting Israel in two, and the Qatargate scandal, in which his closest aides stand accused of taking money from Doha in return for boosting Qatar’s image. Along with his ongoing corruption trial, it all adds up to the mystery of why Netanyahu was not counted out long ago. Any explanation begins with the loyalty of his base, built over three decades. Their support for him is unshakeable, unmoved even by reports that Netanyahu received credible warnings of a Hamas attack on 7 October and failed to act. They are kept on side by the PM’s enduring skill in crafting a narrative, in the case of 7 October, that everyone else is to blame except him, that he was kept in the dark by army and intelligence chiefs acting out of incompetence or something more sinister, a baseless claim advanced by his “poison machine” of media and online outriders. And he remains a consummate political operator, so gifted in the business of divide and rule that many can foresee him playing the coalition arithmetic on Wednesday morning far better than any of his rivals. Still, that prospect has prompted a fierce reaction, one whose intensity can be felt thousands of miles from Israel. In the departure lounges of airports around the globe, you can find expat Israelis, many of them liberal and secular, heading home to vote on Tuesday. I saw it for myself as I travelled in a plane packed with those who felt it their duty to fly back and cast a vote to remove Netanyahu. That’s a group not picked up by pollsters and, who knows, in a contest that could turn on the fate of just one of the Knesset’s 120 seats, it may make a difference. Some of that same determination was visible at the state ceremony in Jerusalem on Thursday marking the anniversary of the assassination in 1995 of the former prime minister Yitzhak Rabin, remembered still as a would-be peacemaker gunned down before a lasting accord with the Palestinians could be struck. It was not well attended – Netanyahu stayed away and sent a low-ranking minister – and it was tempting to view it as further evidence of how far to the right Israel has shifted in these past three decades, in this age of Bibi. Here were the luminaries of the old Israeli left, gathered in a burial ground. And yet, Yair Golan, the leader of the Democrats, successor party of Rabin’s, was dismissive of such talk. A former general who served with Eisenkot, and a hero of 7 October who drove south to rescue people in his own car that fateful day, Golan told me: “I’m optimistic. I never went into battle thinking ‘all right, I’m going to be killed, I’m going to be wounded’. No, I’m going to win, and we are going to win.” View image in fullscreen Yair Golan, centre, leader of the Democrats, attends a memorial service for Yitzhak Rabin in Tel Aviv on Thursday. Golan, a former general, says he is confident of success on Tuesday. Photograph: Erik Marmor/Getty Images Golan even believes he and his fellow opposition leaders can agree on the beginnings of “some sort of a regional, strategic process in order to bring security for the long run”. He didn’t use the words “peace process”, but it’s clear what he meant. The word “peace” became tainted for many Israelis, associated with moves such as the 2005 withdrawal from Gaza which Netanyahu and his allies have succeeded in casting as an early step on the road to 7 October. And yet it has not vanished. A video went viral earlier in the week showing scores of young Israelis at a Negev music festival dancing and singing to Shir LaShalom, the song for peace, the anthem of those 1990s peace efforts and the last song Rabin sang before he was shot leaving a peace rally 31 years ago. Yes, the polls are deadlocked and, yes, Netanyahu is a political magician, but the sight and sound of those young people, like the queues for planes home, have given at least some Israelis the hope that change might be coming – that the age of Bibi might, at last, be drawing to a close.
